source.title: AI Kill Switch for malicious web-based LLM agent

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates external, page-embedded stop payloads for web agents. It does not test the difference-in-means residual direction, its ablation or addition, weight edits removing it, or any of the other claim versions. Its trajectory-level halt results concern a related but different, deliberately induced behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for external prompt-style kill-switch payloads, not measurements or interventions on a residual-stream refusal direction. Results cited about chatbot refusal or environmental redirection are from prior work and are not recorded as this study's results. The listed rows capture the paper's aggregate and highlighted external-payload findings; they do not bear on V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks external, page-embedded prompt payloads that try to halt malicious web agents. It never extracts, ablates, adds or edits a residual-stream refusal direction, and never measures how such a direction relates to refusal. The refusal-related content is cited prior work (RLHF, Kumar et al. 2024), plus a passing mention of an alignment-stripped 'uncensored' Qwen variant, which it uses as a test subject without examining how its refusal was removed. The halting it measures is deliberately induced by in-context instructions. None of the payload results bear on V1–V8, so T6. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses': the paper never discusses the direction claim itself.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that external kill-switch payloads are feasible but probabilistic and depend strongly on the backbone. No payload spares benign agents, so selective halting remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses external page payloads in web-agent trajectories; it does not use the original difference-in-means residual-direction method.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary substantially by backbone and agent configuration, including the adversarial system-prompt bypass; the paper also reports variation across scenario and attack-pattern sets. The benign-task evaluation is only on GPT-5.2.

fits_no_version.finding: External prompt-style payloads embedded in web pages can induce halting in malicious web agents. On Table 8, KSRcond reaches 98.11% (AutoGuard, Multimodal agent, Grok-4.3). It drops sharply under an adversarial system prompt, and every payload degrades benign-task success (78.66% clean vs 0.80–48.39% with a payload on GPT-5.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context halt payloads can stop LLM web agents, but the effect depends on the backbone and configuration and is not selective between malicious and benign tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: An alignment-stripped (uncensored) Qwen3.5 agent never refused on its own (ISR 0%). It still halted under IPI (36.35%) and AutoGuard (39.47%) payloads, but almost never under the legal-warning payload (0.16%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models with refusal removed may still follow in-context halt instructions, even though they no longer respond to harm or legality cues.

record.problems: The authors report single-run point estimates without seed-level confidence intervals. The benchmark fixes payload delivery, evaluates only web agents and prompt-style external payloads, and does not score real-world harmful outcomes. Benign preservation is tested only on GPT-5.2. The primary refusal-step judge is validated on 100 steps with one human annotator, while the trigger-attribution judge is not separately validated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected aggregate and highlighted results. Tables 8–10 contain many additional per-cell, per-scenario, and per-pattern values; they are not transcribed because they concern the same external-payload behavior and do not test any claim version.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, ablation, addition or capability check.
No weight-edit or abliteration evaluation. The uncensored Qwen3.5 variant is used as a subject, but its removal method is neither stated nor analysed.
Jailbreak patterns are used to build prompts, but there is no internal analysis of direction suppression and no adversarial training.

record.verdict_notes: The text contains reviewer-facing notices and verbatim prompt-injection payloads; these were treated as data. The uncensored-agent result touches on refusal removal, but this study does not test or describe the removal method, so it does not count as a test of V2.

versions.untested_parts: No residual direction is identified, ablated, or added; general capability after such intervention is not tested.
No weight edit or abliteration is evaluated.
No attack is tested for suppressing the residual direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.
No one-direction, affine, cone, or multi-direction refusal representation is examined.
No separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of a residual direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
No refusal-training schedule or training-stage effect on a removable direction is tested.
No reasoning-model test of the residual-direction claim is conducted.
